vignette: At twenty, Kwame was navigating the grueling shifts of his first surgical residency, but his mind remained trapped in the arid hills of the eastern patrol zone six months prior. He remembered the ambush not as a coherent sequence but as a violent rupture. One moment he was scanning the ridge, the next, small-arms fire erupted, followed by a deafening blast that threw him into the dirt. The dust choked him, pressing against his chest until he could barely draw air, and for a terrifying stretch, the battlefield fell into an absolute, ringing silence. When the noise returned, it was the sound of men falling and weapons barking in rapid succession. He survived, but the ground beneath his feet had given way. He began walking the hospital corridors with his shoulders permanently drawn up, scanning exits and monitoring the rhythm of every breath in the waiting rooms. He couldn't explain it, but he was certain the world had fundamentally broken, and the man who used to step onto the line was gone, replaced by someone who no longer recognized his own hands or his own purpose. Within weeks, the clinical setting transformed from a place of healing into a minefield. When a resident collapsed in the ICU, gasping for air, Kwame's own chest tightened reflexively, the familiar panic of suffocation surging before he could steady himself. The sudden hush over the nurses' station after a code blue triggered a cold spike in his stomach, echoing that dead air on the ridge. Even the muffled thud of a gurney wheel made him flinch toward the noise. Each time his body recoiled, it felt less like a reflex and more like confirmation. The breathlessness, the silence, the violence-all proof that his previous understanding of safety had been an illusion. He was convinced that if he ever let his guard down again, the same collapse would happen to everyone he cared for, and that he was fundamentally broken for feeling so paralyzed by it. That unshakable conviction fractured his recall. When he tried to reconstruct the patrol, his mind deliberately shoved the image away before it could fully materialize, leaving only jagged shards that refused to align. He would sit in the hospital lot, gripping the steering wheel, trying to force the timeline together, but large sections simply vanished. The more his thoughts looped on his shattered worldview and relentless mental scanning, the more his memory retreated behind an impenetrable wall. His hypervigilance didn't just keep him awake; it actively suppressed the very memories he needed to process, forcing him to abandon the narrative before his brain could finish compiling it. Conversely, those very gaps bred a corrosive doubt that deepened his negative self-appraisals. He kept circling back to the blank spaces, wondering what he had failed to see, which only reinforced his conviction that he could no longer trust himself or the reality he thought he knew. The missing pieces felt like evidence of a deeper failure, constantly reminding him that he was fundamentally compromised and that his identity had been hollowed out by the event. Every time he confronted those absences, his shattered beliefs about permanence and control hardened further, leaving him isolated and certain that he had lost himself entirely. The unresolved fragments and the holes in his timeline kept his nervous system perpetually armed. Because he could not anchor the event in a complete narrative, his body remained stuck in the waiting period before the blast, his lungs automatically hitching in preparation for impact whenever the ward grew still or a monitor flatlined. His relentless mental scanning and conviction that the world was permanently unsafe turned every ordinary hospital moment into a threat. Because he braced for catastrophe, a sudden quiet in the hall felt like a loaded weapon, and any heavy breathing in the corridor immediately spiked his own breathlessness. Memory gaps did not just distort the past; they wired him to anticipate the next strike, making every sudden movement feel like the opening act of the same disaster. By his fourth month in residency, the exhaustion of constant scanning had begun to compromise his clinical judgment. He caught himself staring blankly during rounds, his breathing shallow despite the clean environment. He finally walked into the campus counseling center because his attending noticed his hesitation before a procedure and his pupils were blown wide despite the overhead lights. He sat on the edge of the chair now, wondering if the man who left for deployment would ever step back out of the room, or if he was permanently fractured. He hoped for a way to breathe again without bracing for the next explosion, and feared that he might never be able to look at a silent room or steady his own hands long enough to hold a scalpel.
